title: Non-specific defences; Antibodies, primary/secondary responses and immunity types
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: IM02#t2 term and clue written for the game; IM02#t4 term and clue written for the game; IM04#t2 term and clue written for the game; IM04#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: IM02#N.9, IM04#N.3, IM02#N.11, IM04#N.9, IM02#N.13.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Endocytosis
items.clue: Engulfing process that encloses the pathogen in a vesicle.

items.label: Amoeboid movement
items.clue: How defensive cells squeeze out of capillaries to reach the infection site.

items.label: Agglutination
items.clue: Clumping of pathogens, linked together by molecules that each have two binding sites.

items.label: Antibody
items.clue: Protein made by plasma cells, with a binding site complementary to one specific target.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the innate immune system from the adaptive immune system?

options.text: Both systems build up a memory of the pathogens they meet, but the innate system does so faster because it does not need to be specific to each one.
The innate system is the specific one, with each phagocyte recognising just a single type of pathogen, while the lymphocytes respond to broad categories of pathogen.
The innate system responds to broad categories of pathogen and does not change during life; the adaptive system is specific and builds a memory of pathogens.
The adaptive system responds faster than the innate system on first exposure to a pathogen, because a specific response is a more efficient response.

questions.explanation: The innate response (including phagocytes) is the same on every exposure, whereas the adaptive response is specific to particular pathogens and becomes more effective because a memory of pathogens encountered is retained.

questions.stem: Antibodies against measles and antibodies against tetanus toxin are compared. Which part of the molecule differs between them?

options.text: The disulfide bridges, which create a different binding site in each antibody.
The constant region, which is shaped to fit the antigen.
The variable region, which forms the antigen-binding site.
The number of polypeptide chains, which depends on the size of the antigen.

questions.explanation: Different amino acid sequences in the variable regions give different binding sites, each complementary to its own antigen.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how a phagocyte destroys a bacterium?

options.text: It secretes enzymes from its lysosomes onto the bacterium, digesting it outside the cell, and then absorbs the soluble products.
It engulfs the bacterium by endocytosis and then digests it inside the cell, using the enzymes from its lysosomes.
It lets the bacterium pass straight through its plasma membrane into the cytoplasm, where cytoplasmic enzymes break it down.
It binds to the bacterium using a receptor specific to that strain and holds it until lymphocytes arrive to destroy it.

questions.explanation: Phagocytes recognise pathogens, engulf them by endocytosis so that the pathogen is enclosed in a vesicle, and digest them using enzymes from lysosomes that fuse with the vesicle.

questions.stem: What is the basis of a person's immunity to a disease that they have previously had?

options.text: Memory cells that are specific to the pathogen survive long-term and can make the antibodies that are needed.
Antibodies made during the first infection remain in the blood at a protective level for the rest of the person's life.
Memory cells are plasma cells that keep on secreting the antibody at a low rate for many years after the infection.
Phagocytes of the innate immune system learned to recognise the pathogen during the first infection and now destroy it faster.

questions.explanation: Immunity is the ability to eliminate an infectious disease from the body. It is due to the long-term survival of lymphocytes that are capable of making the specific antibodies needed: memory cells.

questions.stem: In a phagocyte, the lysosomes cannot fuse with phagosomes, but every other step works normally. What happens to a bacterium that meets this phagocyte?

options.text: It is engulfed, then digested in the cytoplasm by enzymes released from the phagosome.
It is digested outside the cell instead, by lysosomal enzymes secreted onto it.
It is not engulfed, because engulfing depends on lysosomes.
It is engulfed but survives inside the phagosome, as no enzymes reach it.

questions.explanation: Engulfing and digesting are separate steps. Without fusion, the enzymes never reach the bacterium.
